How do we pick the weights?
How do we pick the weights?
One option is preference elicitation.
Candy Example
We want to learn a weight vector over the following three candies:
1.  M&Ms (w1​)
2.  Sour Patch Kids (w2​)
3.  Skittles (w3​)
w=[w1​,w2​,w3​]
We will do so using pairwise queries.
Candy Example
Since w1​+w2​+w3​=1, we can plot the set of possible weights using only w1​ and w2​.

In this case, we preselected the queries. We would probably do better if we selected the queries as we went to maximize the amount of information they provide! (lots of research on preference-based learning, beyond the scope of this class)
We also assumed that the expert was perfectly rational. It is common to relax this assumption and instead compute a distribution over the weights. (beyond the scope of this class)

Example
Express the following statement using propositional logic:
“If the agent is in a safe state, then the agent is not in a collision state”
Atomic propositions:
S: the agent is in a safe state
C: the agent is in a collision state

First-Order Logic
First-Order Logic
First-order logic adds variables, predicates, and quantifiers to propositional logic.
First-Order Logic
First-order logic adds variables, predicates, and quantifiers to propositional logic.
variable: object in a domain
e.g. let the variable x represent the state of an agent
First-Order Logic
First-order logic adds variables, predicates, and quantifiers to propositional logic.
variable: object in a domain
e.g. let the variable x represent the state of an agent
predicate: function that evaluates propositions over variables
e.g. the predicate P(x) returns true if the agent is in a safe state,
and the predicate Q(x) returns true if the agent is in a collision state.
Example
“If the agent is in a safe state, then the agent is not in a collision state”
P(x)→¬Q(x)
First-Order Logic
First-order logic adds variables, predicates, and quantifiers to propositional logic.
quantifiers allow us to evaluate propositions over a collection of variables
Universal Quantifier ∀ (“for all”): all variables must satisfy the proposition.
e.g. “all states are safe states” is written as ∀x P(x)
Existential Quantifier ∃ (“there exists”): at least one variable in the domain satisfies the proposition.
e.g. “at least one state is a safe state” is written as ∃x P(x)
First-Order Logic
Example
“for all states in the trajectory, the
agent does not hit an obstacle”
O(x): x is an obstacle state
ψ1​=∀x ¬O(x)
First-Order Logic
Example
“the agent must reach a goal state and
avoid the obstacle state.”
O(x): x is an obstacle state
G(x): x is a goal state
ψ2​=(∀x ¬O(x))∧(∃x G(x))

Temporal Logic

Temporal Logic
Properties over linear sequences of states:
□P
“always P”
\square
“P is true at all time
steps in the future”
◊P
“eventually P”
\lozenge
“P is true at some time
step in the future”
PUQ
“P until Q”
“Q is true at some time step in
the future and P is true at least
until Q becomes true.”
